content: A chevron plot is a graphical representation used to analyze protein folding kinetics under varying concentrations of denaturants, which are chemical agents that disrupt the native tertiary structure of proteins. The plot is named chevron because it typically exhibits a V-shaped or chevron-like appearance when the logarithm of the observed relaxation rate is plotted against the concentration of the denaturant. In a two-state folding system, the observed relaxation rates are primarily governed by the folding and unfolding rates of the protein. These rates dominate below and above the denaturation midpoint (Cm), respectively. This characteristic gives rise to the terminology of folding arm and unfolding arm for the two limbs of the chevron plot. The Cm of a protein can often be determined beforehand through equilibrium experiments. When fitting the data to a two-state model, it is assumed that the logarithms of the folding and unfolding rates vary linearly with the concentration of the denaturant. This linear dependence results in slopes referred to as the folding (mf) and unfolding (mu) m-values, also known as kinetic m-values. The sum of the folding and unfolding rates corresponds to the observed relaxation rate. Agreement between the equilibrium m-value and the absolute sum of the kinetic m-values is typically considered a hallmark of two-state folding behavior. Most denaturation experiments reported in the literature are conducted at 298 K, using either urea or guanidinium chloride (GuHCl) as the denaturants. To generate the folding arm of the chevron plot, the protein is initially dissolved in a highly concentrated denaturant solution. This solution is then rapidly diluted (within less than a millisecond) into an appropriate buffer to achieve a specific denaturant concentration. This process is typically performed using a stopped-flow apparatus. The relaxation of the protein to its new equilibrium state is monitored using spectroscopic probes, such as fluorescence, or less commonly, circular dichroism (CD). The dilution volume is carefully adjusted to measure the relaxation rate at a specific denaturant concentration. The final protein concentration in the mixture is usually maintained between 1 and 20 µM, depending on the constraints imposed by the relaxation amplitude and the signal-to-noise ratio. The unfolding arm of the chevron plot is generated in a similar manner by mixing a denaturant-free protein solution with a concentrated denaturant solution in buffer. When the logarithm of the relaxation rates is plotted as a function of the final denaturant concentration, the characteristic chevron plot is obtained. The mixing process determines the dead time of the instrument, which is typically around one millisecond. Consequently, a stopped-flow apparatus is suitable only for proteins with relaxation times on the order of a few milliseconds. For proteins with relaxation times shorter than the instrument's dead time, the experimental temperature is lowered to increase the relaxation time by increasing the viscosity of the water or buffer. Alternatively, techniques such as temperature-jump (T-jump, with dead times on the order of nanoseconds) or continuous-flow mixing (with dead times on the order of microseconds) can be employed to study proteins with relaxation rates in the range of 1–100 microseconds. These methods can be used at different denaturant concentrations to construct a chevron plot. Although the limbs of the chevron plot are generally assumed to be linear with respect to denaturant concentration, deviations from linearity, known as chevron roll-overs, are sometimes observed. These roll-overs can occur in one or both limbs of the plot. The underlying causes of chevron roll-overs are not fully understood, but several explanations have been proposed, including the presence of on-pathway intermediates, limitations due to instrument dead time, shifts in the transition state (Hammond effect), aggregation artifacts, downhill folding, and salt-induced Debye-Hückel effects. In many cases, folding limb roll-overs are ignored because they occur at low denaturant concentrations, and the data are fit to a two-state model assuming linear dependence of the rates. However, this approach can lead to an overestimation of the folding rates reported for such proteins in the absence of denaturants.
